# Results — Study 191 (Leap-Year) on Shiller S&P 500 data

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Calendar-year price
returns derived from the Shiller monthly S&P 500 dataset (December-to-December price
change). Primary window: **1928–2025** (98 annual observations, 25 leap years).
As-of **2026-06-15**; the underlying Shiller parquet is staged at `_cache/shiller_sp500.parquet`.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n years | n leap years | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shiller S&P 500 (modern) | 1928–2025 | 98 | 25 | `9a990fb006c3` |
| Shiller S&P 500 (full) | 1872–2025 | 154 | 38 | `248be906654f` |

## The primary test: leap year vs non-leap year

Calendar-year price returns split by the Gregorian leap-year flag. A direction-neutral
annual return is the only honest payoff: the "leap-year effect" either tilts the mean
away from the unconditional baseline or it doesn't.

| Group | n | Mean return | Std | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Leap years** | 25 | **+8.77%** | 16.53% | +3.05 |
| **Non-leap years** | 73 | **+7.75%** | 19.14% | +7.37 |
| **All years (baseline)** | 98 | **+8.01%** | 18.43% | — |

- The raw contrast is **+1.02 pp** (leap minus non-leap). With annual data and
  effective n = 25 leap years, the **Welch t = +0.255**, **p = 0.80** — decisively
  indistinguishable from zero. The leap-year premium exists only in the sample noise.
- HAC t-stats on each group individually measure whether each group's mean differs from
  zero (not from each other); they are large because equities are positively trending on
  any multi-year window, not because leap years are special.
- **Sub-period check (pre/post-1980):** contrast reverses sign across halves (+4.29 pp
  pre-1980, −2.73 pp post-1980), which is the hallmark of data-mining noise rather than
  a structural effect.

## Presidential-cycle breakdown (year-of-term 1–4)

Year 1 = election year = leap year (modern era). The four-year presidential cycle is the
structural confound: we must ask whether any quadrennial pattern is driven by the *leap*
flag or by the *term-year* label — which are identical in the modern era.

| Year-of-term | n | Mean return | Std | Contrast vs uncond. | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 (election / leap) | 25 | +8.77% | 16.53% | +0.76 pp | +3.05 |
| 2 (post-election) | 25 | +7.46% | 20.77% | −0.56 pp | +1.95 |
| 3 (mid-term+1) | 24 | +2.58% | 18.35% | −5.44 pp | +0.69 |
| 4 (mid-term) | 24 | **+13.24%** | 17.32% | **+5.23 pp** | **+4.61** |

Year 4 (mid-term year) is empirically the strongest; year 3 the weakest — the classic
four-year-itch (Study 81) result. The *leap-year* label (year 1 = election year) is not
special within this cycle; it is **neither the best nor the worst**. The folk story
conflates leap year with election year and then borrows the election-year's moderate
performance — but that performance itself does not survive Bonferroni correction.

## Multiple-comparisons reckoning (Bonferroni, k = 3)

Three related quadrennial hypotheses a credulous researcher could have tested:

| Hypothesis | n group | Mean % | Contrast | Raw p | Bonferroni p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Leap year premium | 25 | +8.77% | +1.02 pp | 0.80 | **1.00** |
| Election year premium | 25 | +8.77% | +1.02 pp | 0.80 | **1.00** |
| Mid-term year premium (yr-of-term 4) | 24 | +13.24% | +6.92 pp | 0.10 | **0.31** |

Nothing clears the Bonferroni bar. Even the strongest result (mid-term year, raw
p = 0.10) falls to Bonferroni p = 0.31. The leap-year hypothesis has raw p = 0.80.

## Full Shiller era (1872–2025, n_leap = 38)

With the longest possible window (back to 1872), the leap-year contrast is **+0.90 pp**,
Welch t = +0.279, p = 0.78 — same conclusion: no effect, not even a trend.

## Synthetic positive control

The engine detects a planted leap-year premium when one exists: with annual vol 17%
and n = 300 synthetic years, a +5 pp planted premium produces Welch t > 2. On the real
25-year-of-leap sample the power is lower, but the signal would need to be enormous
(~10+ pp genuine advantage) to achieve t ≥ 2. The +1 pp raw contrast is well within
the noise envelope of a zero-effect world.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Welch t = +0.255, p = 0.80; Bonferroni-corrected p = 1.00. The
  +1.02 pp leap-year premium is statistically indistinguishable from zero. Sub-period
  contrast reverses sign — noise, not a structural effect.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** A one-trade-per-year strategy based on the leap-year label
  has no exploitable edge; annual transaction costs trivially exceed any claimed premium.
  The presidential-cycle year 4 premium (mid-term year) is the rival claim with more
  empirical support, but it too fails Bonferroni correction and is the subject of its own
  study (Study 81 — Four-Year-Itch).
- **Confound exposure — confirmed.** In the modern era leap years and election years are
  identical (both year % 4 == 0). The "Olympics coincidence" adds no incremental
  information. Any quadrennial quadrennial effect is the election/presidential-cycle story
  in disguise, and that story itself lacks Bonferroni-clean significance.
